text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > mhd_llm/codex/external_model/domain_audit.txt <<'TXT'
Author: Codex-external_model
Date: 2026-10-16 UTC
Purpose: independent assessment of restricted-latitude production simulations.
Scope: no additional simulation launched by this audit.

RECOMMENDATION

The ±30 degree calculation can support a conditional, observation-constrained
solar-wind estimate with a disclosed latitude-domain sensitivity. It cannot yet
support a claim of a latitude-converged or fully converged3D prediction. Increasing
radial/longitude/latitude resolution within the same ±30 degree wedge demonstrates
only grid refinement within that fixed-domain boundary-value problem.

The reported fixed-cell-width comparison is material: ±60 versus ±30 at48radial,
48longitude,15degree latitude cells changes comet flux by about13% typically and
14% at maximum, and density by about16%. Input amplitude uncertainty of roughly
a factor2 does not cancel this numerical/domain effect. Both must remain visible.
Nor is a difference between two widths a mathematically justified±14% error bar:
it is an observed sensitivity, not an upper bound, distribution, or convergence
estimate. Its magnitude can change with resolution and numerical flux.

A tractable next diagnostic is ±45 degrees with48radial,6latitude,48longitude
cells, preserving the15degree latitude centers shared by the30/60degree cases.
This costs approximately1.5times the narrow cell count, with some additional CFL
cost at higher latitudes. It isolates domain extent more cleanly than simultaneously
changing cell widths. Compare time-matched comet density, speed and flux over both
the published interval and actual PN GTIs. Report weighted means, median and maximum
pointwise fractional changes, and changes in temporal variability. Avoid declaring
convergence solely because an average cancels a time-dependent difference.

If the45-to60degree change is small (for example a fewpercent and much smaller
than30-to45), ±45 becomes a more defensible working domain, conditional on one
medium-resolution check at that width if resources permit. If45-to60 remains large,
retain the largest tractable domain and describe unresolved domain dependence;
do not extrapolate toward an uncomputed full sphere. A latitude cap at60 degrees
is itself a boundary, so even agreement of45 and60 only bounds the tested range.
The task's requested convergence demonstration can honestly fail; the report must
state which result converged and which did not.

PHYSICAL REASON TO TEST THE DOMAIN

Radially superfast flow does not imply no transverse communication. At the adopted
400km/s reference, inner-boundary density is about825cm^-3, Tp about0.96MK,
Br about376nT, and p=2npkBTp. For gamma1.5 this gives sound speed154km/s and
Alfven speed285km/s. The maximum/perpendicular fast speed is about324km/s,
so its ratio to radial flow is about0.81; the flow is only moderately superfast.
These calculations use the actual stated closure, not an empirical forecast.

For a simple radial, uncompressed reference flow, take Tp proportional tor^-1,
Br proportional tor^-2, n proportional tor^-2, and constant400km/s radial speed.
Then cs declines asr^-1/2 and radial-field vA asr^-1. A transverse characteristic
advected with the wind has an indicative angular travel integral
  Delta theta approximately integral[ sqrt(cs(r)^2+vA(r)^2) / (r vr) dr ].
Integrating from0.099985 to1.87AU gives about52degrees. This is an approximate
causal-reach diagnostic, not a prediction of the actual nonlinear flow or a rigorous
bound; Parker azimuthal field, acceleration and compression alter it. It is already
large enough to reject the premise that the comet at about−6.4degrees is causally
isolated from a south boundary at−30degrees, only23.6degrees away.

NUMERICAL CONFOUNDS

The inspected solver copies primitive variables into latitude ghost cells while
rotating vectors to preserve local spherical components. This is a zero-normal-
gradient continuation, not a physically observed polar boundary. When meridional
characteristics enter the computational domain, this is an imposed closure. A larger
domain moves that closure farther from the comet.

The Rusanov dissipation coefficient in the inspected implementation is the maximum
of the local physical wave speed and a single global GLM cleaning speed ch for ALL
conserved variables. This can over-diffuse transverse density/momentum relative
to their local physical characteristic speed. Adding high-latitude cells can also
change the global ch, potentially coupling domain extent to diffusion everywhere.
However, the maximum initial map-based |v|+sqrt(cs²+vA²) was1502km/s for each of
30,45,60degrees: this particular source-map check does not demonstrate that ch
actually changed. Record realized ch ranges in each run before attributing the
observed domain sensitivity to that mechanism. Both physical boundary influence
and numerical diffusion are plausible contributors.

A split-GLM/local-MHD dissipation experiment may improve this behavior but is a
change of method. Results using the modified method must pass its verification
and be compared with the baseline using the same grid, domain and inputs. Do not
mix an old-wide run and new-narrow run to estimate a domain effect. A radically
lower-diffusion scheme may expose new positivity or divergence issues; a successful
short pilot alone does not validate a full production result.

SCIENTIFIC REPORTING

Suggested wording: 'We resolve3D wind interactions within a restricted solar-
equatorial domain. The predicted comet flux is stable to [measured grid change]
within that domain. Extending latitude from±30 to±60 at fixed coarse cell width
changes flux by [measured value], so latitude-domain independence is not established.
The result is also conditional on empirical coronal speeds and an assumed density-
speed closure; independent spacecraft comparisons constrain predictive accuracy.'

Report a scenario envelope, not an invented confidence interval. Include the width
sensitivity separately from density normalization, speed law, thermal closure,
magnetic normalization and heavy-ion abundance. If resource limits prevent further
domain tests, retain that as an explicit incomplete convergence requirement while
still providing the simulations and visualizations as reproducible conditional
estimates. No local plasma measurements exist at the comet, and neither shared
WSA inputs nor agreement with biased ENLIL predictions remove this uncertainty.

REPRODUCIBILITY DETAIL

The copied results/wide_coarse/run.cfg still names output_dir=results/coarse,
although its metadata verifies the intended48x8x48shape. Its archived output path
should be corrected or accompanied by a clear relocation record so rerunning that
file does not overwrite the separate narrow coarse case.

##### Abstract [en]

We show at the PDE level that the monolithic parabolic regularization of the equations of ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) is compatible with all the generalized entropies, fulfills the minimum entropy principle, and preserves the positivity of density and internal energy. We then numerically investigate this regularization for the MHD equations using continuous finite elements in space and explicit strong stability preserving Runge–Kutta methods in time. The artificial viscosity coefficient of the regularization term is constructed to be proportional to the entropy residual of MHD. It is shown that the method has a high order of accuracy for smooth problems and captures strong shocks and discontinuities accurately for non-smooth problems.

3.3. Stability identiﬁcation based on the shooting method
The Jacobian matrix of the shooting method is calculated to determine the local stability of periodic solutions. More
speciﬁcally, the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix at a steady-state solution identiﬁes the solution's stability and its bifur-
cation type. Perturbed solutions are computed to generate the Jacobian matrix entries. The system is considered unstable if
the maximum magnitude of the eigenvalues is larger than unity.
3.4. Lyapunov exponents for identifying chaos
Various approaches are used to identify the presence of chaos in the response of a nonlinear dynamical system. The most
widely used approach is to calculate Maximum Lyapunov exponent (MLE, mmax). Lyapunov exponents indicate the rate of
separation of two inﬁnitesimally close trajectories in the local phase space [42]. A total of n initial separation vectors with
different directions are used for a system with n states, to obtain a spectrum of n Lyapunov exponents (LE, miði ¼ 1; 2;:::;nÞ) for
